# hr9917-ai-kill-switch-act-bill-text
- **URL:** https://www.congress.gov/119/bills/hr9917/BILLS-119hr9917ih.pdf (PDF downloaded and text-extracted; congress.gov HTML returned 403) · **Accessed:** 2026-09-16 · **For:** v1 response round, Finding H (scope; whether it touches users)
- **What it establishes:** H.R. 9917 adds new sec. 2220F to the Homeland Security Act. "Covered entity" (the operative term; the release says "covered developers") = an entity that operates a covered technology or a system incorporating it, makes it available to third parties "through a programmatic interface, hosted service, or other similar mechanism," and derives with affiliates "not less than $500,000,000 in gross revenue from such technology" in the prior year. "Covered technology" = an AI system trained with compute costing over "$100,000,000 at the prevailing market price of cloud computing." Exemption for "personal, academic, or non-commercial utilization only." DHS must update the definitions by rule annually, considering among other factors "the manner in which the model weights of such technology are made available." Required capabilities: stop inference, "Terminate user access," "Suspend access ... with respect to an account, user, or use pattern identified by such covered entity or the Secretary as posing a risk," and "Shut down such technology"; incident report within 15 days. Emergency authority: DHS Secretary "in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence" may order proportionate action; the entity must "Preserve the model weights and telemetry," notify operators/users, and confirm; DHS verifies "through audit, telemetry, on-site inspection, or other forensic review"; 48-hour petition, D.C. Circuit review. "Covered incident" includes sabotage of a shutdown instruction, unintended conduct causing 10+ deaths or $100M damages, concealment from a monitoring/shutdown mechanism, and a "loss-of-control scenario." It does NOT reach consumer devices or locally run weights; but it does reach users indirectly, through mandated account-level termination/suspension capabilities that the Secretary may trigger.
- **Key passages:**
  - "(ii) Terminate user access to such technology. (iii) Suspend access to such technology with respect to an account, user, or use pattern identified by such covered entity or the Secretary as posing a risk"
  - "Derives together with the affiliates, if any, of such person not less than $500,000,000 in gross revenue from such technology"
  - "developed utilizing a quantity of computing power the cost of which would exceed $100,000,000 at the prevailing market price of cloud computing in the United States"
  - "Preserve the model weights and telemetry of such technology."
  - "the manner in which the model weights of such technology are made available" (rulemaking factor)
- **Reliability:** Primary (introduced bill text, "IH" version).
- **Relevance to this project:** Corrects the editor on scope: the bill is developer/operator-facing and does not touch consumer devices, but it explicitly mandates per-user and per-account suspension capabilities and lets DHS identify the accounts. Also the open-weights question is deferred to rulemaking, not exempted.

## Added 2026-09-16 (v2→v3 response round, slice K; whole 15-page IH PDF re-read page by page via curl + PDF reader)
- **Identity:** H.R. 9917, 119th Cong., 2d Sess., introduced July 23, 2026 by Mr. Lieu (for himself and Mr. Moran), referred to House Homeland Security. Sec. 2 adds new "SEC. 2220F" to Subtitle A of title XXII of the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (6 U.S.C. 651 et seq.). All cites below are to new § 2220F; page/line = IH print.
- **(a) Appeal — § 2220F(c)(5) (p. 7 l.18 – p. 8 l.14). CONFIRMED verbatim:**
  - (c)(5)(A): "Not later than 48 hours after an order under paragraph (1), the covered entity subject to such order may petition the Secretary for reconsideration of such order, but such petition does not stay such order."
  - (c)(5)(B): "Not later than five days after a covered entity petitions pursuant to subparagraph (A), the Secretary, acting through the Director, shall make a determination with respect to such petition, but if the Secretary fails to so make such determination, such failure is deemed to be a determination in the negative."
  - (c)(5)(C): "A covered entity for which there is an order under paragraph (1) may request review of such order in the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit on petition filed not later than 60 days after such order."
  - The bill sets NO timetable for the court, NO expedited review, NO stay provision, and no standard of review. The only "within days" events are administrative (48 h to petition; 5 days for the Secretary, silence = denial). Only the *covered entity* may petition or seek review; users/operators get notice ((c)(2)(B)) but no review right. So "reviewable in court within days" is wrong: 60 days is a filing deadline for the company, not a decision deadline for anyone.
- **(b) Account-level suspension — (b)(1)(A)(iii) (p. 4 l.5–12). CONFIRMED verbatim:** "(iii) Suspend access to such technology with respect to an account, user, or use pattern identified by such covered entity or the Secretary as posing a risk of any of the following: (I) A covered incident. (II) A violation of law or the terms of service of such technology." This is a *capability the rule must require the entity to maintain*. The emergency order in (c)(1) "may include any of the actions described in subsection (b)(1)(A)" but is triggered only when the Secretary "determines that a covered incident has occurred" (not on a ToS violation alone). Precision point: the ToS/"violation of law" trigger lives in the capability mandate; the statutory order power is keyed to an occurred covered incident.
- **(c) Annual redefinition — (a)(1)–(2) (p. 2 l.12 – p. 3 l.12). CONFIRMED:** "(1) ... not later than 90 days after the date of the enactment of this section and annually thereafter, the Secretary, acting through the Director, shall update by rule the definitions for the terms 'covered entity' and 'covered technology' in this section." Factors (a)(2): (A) small-business burden; (B) "The need to cover entities the activities of which have the potential to advance artificial intelligence capabilities in national security, including with respect to cybersecurity and chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear capabilities."; (C) "The capabilities of covered technology, the deployment of such technology, and the manner in which the model weights of such technology are made available."; (D) "Such other factors as the Secretary determines relevant."
- **(d) Definitions — (g)(4), (g)(6), (a)(3). CONFIRMED:** (g)(4) covered entity = "(A) Operates a covered technology or operates a system that incorporates such technology. (B) Makes such technology available to a third party through a programmatic interface, hosted service, or other similar mechanism. (C) Derives together with the affiliates, if any, of such person not less than $500,000,000 in gross revenue from such technology in the calendar year preceding the calendar year at issue." All three are conjunctive ("satisfies the following requirements"). (g)(6) covered technology = "an artificial intelligence system developed utilizing a quantity of computing power the cost of which would exceed $100,000,000 at the prevailing market price of cloud computing in the United States, as determined by the Secretary." (a)(3): "An entity is not a covered entity if such entity operates or makes available to a third party a covered technology for personal, academic, or non-commercial utilization only." Both statutory definitions open "Except as otherwise provided in this section" — i.e., subject to the (a)(1) rulemaking.
- **(e) Throttling — (b)(2)(A)(i) (p. 4 l.18 – p. 5 l.20). CONFIRMED:** throttling appears only under "(2) CONSIDERATION.—In carrying out paragraph (1), the Secretary shall consider the following: (A) Requiring a technical capability based on a graduated deployment-corrections framework that applies when there is evidence of a credible risk of a covered incident and includes measures that are calibrated to the severity and immediacy of such risk, including ... (i) Throttling or otherwise altering any of the following: (I) The inference rate of a covered technology. (II) User access to such technology. (III) Compute allocation with respect to such technology. (ii) Disabling or restricting a capability ... (iii) Suspending ... (iv) Shutting down ... (v) Transitioning an operation dependent on such technology to a backup system or an earlier version". The mandatory list in (b)(1)(A) is only: stop inference; terminate user access; suspend account/user/use pattern; shut down. Note the graduated framework's trigger is "evidence of a credible risk", lower than the order's "has occurred".
- **(f) Preservation and verification — (c)(2)–(3) (p. 6 l.12 – p. 7 l.7). CONFIRMED:** on an order the entity "shall as soon as practicable": "(A) Preserve the model weights and telemetry of such technology. (B) Notify to the extent practicable each operator or user of such technology, of ... (i) Such order. (ii) The extent to which such operator or user ... might be affected by such order. (C) Confirm to the Secretary that such order has been carried out." (c)(3): the Secretary "shall through audit, telemetry, on-site inspection, or other forensic review verify compliance". "Telemetry" is NOT defined anywhere in the bill.
- **(g) Remaining provisions. CONFIRMED:**
  - Covered incident (g)(5): "an occurrence of any of the following outside of red-teaming or other structured testing: (A) Sabotage of, or interference with, a lawful instruction to shut down a covered technology. (B) Conduct of such technology that is unintended by a developer or operator of such technology and causes the death of not fewer than 10 individuals or economic damages of not less than $100,000,000. (C) Concealment of a capability, intention, or action of such technology, by such technology, from a monitoring or shutdown mechanism. (D) A loss-of-control scenario." Loss-of-control (g)(7) includes "(D) Such technology attaining without such authorization access to the model weights of such technology."
  - Order (c)(1): Secretary "acting through the Director and in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, determines that a covered incident has occurred ... may order the covered entity at issue to take action proportionate to the nature and immediacy of such incident".
  - FOIA (f): "Nonpublic information submitted under this section to the Secretary by a covered entity is exempt from disclosure under section 552(b)(3) of title 5 ... and from any provision of State, local, or Tribal freedom of information law".
  - Penalties (d)(2): up to "$2,000,000 for each day" for violating the section; up to "$20,000,000 for each day" for violating subsection (c); both "after reasonable notice and opportunity for a hearing"; (d)(1) subpoena and investigation power, incl. outside the U.S.; (d)(3) AG civil action; (e) 30-day cure for de minimis/technical defects.
  - Congressional report on each order (c)(4). Voluntary shutdown standards within 180 days (b)(3).
  - **No sunset clause** anywhere (read end to end; the only time limits are 90 days/annually, 180 days, 15 days, 48 hours, five days, 60 days, 30 days).
- **What the bill does NOT contain (checked by full read):** no requirement to log, retain, or hand over *user content* or prompts; the only data-preservation duty is "model weights and telemetry" on an order, with "telemetry" undefined (so a sentence saying the bill mandates retention of conversations would be unsupported; a sentence saying it leaves the door open via undefined "telemetry" and DHS "forensic review" is defensible). No express mention of open-weight / open-source models beyond the (a)(2)(C) rulemaking factor. No mention of consumer devices, chips, or local inference; "hardware" appears only inside the definition of "artificial intelligence system" ((g)(3)(B)). The revenue test and the hosted-service test mean a pure weights publisher with no hosted service is outside the statutory definition as introduced, but the Secretary can redefine "covered entity" annually.
